blocks.text: Appendix Set One: Technical Reference Tables

blocks.h: This appendix contains five technical reference tables designed for use alongside the main text of this work. They are intended as quick-reference tools for practitioners, CIIN examination candidates, and insurers building compliance documentation.
• Table 1A: EFU Nigerian Life Mortality Table — Illustrative Extract (ages 20–70)

blocks.text: Table 1A: EFU Nigerian Life Mortality Table — Illustrative Extract

blocks.h: The EFU (Experience Follows Up) Nigerian Life Tables are based on the mortality experience of Nigerian insured lives, compiled and published periodically by NAICOM in collaboration with the Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria (IAN). The qx values in this appendix are a representative illustrative extract showing the structure and format of the EFU life table.

For actual product pricing, reserving, actuarial investigations, and regulatory filings, practitioners must use the current officially endorsed EFU table. Access the current endorsed version from: NAICOM (naicom.gov.ng — actuarial resources section); the Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria (IAN); or through your company’s Statutory Actuary. Do not use this illustrative extract for any live actuarial calculation.

The EFU Nigerian Life Table expresses mortality as a probability: qx is the probability that a life aged exactly x will die before reaching age x+1. The complement (px = 1 – qx) is the probability of surviving the year. The lx column shows the number of survivors from a notional cohort of 100,000 lives at age 0; dx shows deaths at each age. The êx column shows the curtate expectation of life — the expected number of complete future years of life remaining.
Key concepts for reading the table:

items.h: qx: Mortality rate at age x. Increases with age. Nigerian insured lives show lower qx than the general population at most ages due to the insurance selection effect.
1,000qx: The mortality rate expressed per 1,000 lives — the more intuitive form used in comparative analysis (e.g., ‘2.3 per 1,000’ at age 30).
lx: Number alive at exact age x from a radix of 100,000 (l0 = 100,000). Obtained by l(x+1) = lx × (1 – qx).
dx: Deaths in the year of age x to x+1. dx = lx × qx. The total of all dx values equals 100,000 (the radix).
êx: Curtate life expectancy at age x — expected number of complete future years. A 35-year-old with ê35 = 38.2 is expected to live, on average, 38 more complete years (to approximately age 73).

blocks.h: Notes: Shaded rows (blue) indicate decennial ages (20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70) for quick reference. Values are illustrative of the EFU table format. qx values follow a Makeham-Gompertz progression appropriate for Nigerian insured lives. Source: Illustrative extract modelled on EFU(N) table structure. For live use, obtain current NAICOM-endorsed version from naicom.gov.ng or the Institute of Actuaries of Nigeria.

blocks.text: Table 1B: NIIRA 2025 Minimum Paid-Up Capital Thresholds

rows: Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (Act No. 2, 2025), Part II.
NAICOM Recapitalisation Directive (implementing circular) specifies the phased compliance timeline for existing licensees.
The fully paid and non-encumbered share capital that a licensee must maintain at all times. Unpaid subscription, share application money not yet allotted, and deferred shares do not qualify.
NAICOM confirms capital adequacy through the annual statutory return. Capital must be maintained continuously, not merely at a single point-in-time measurement.
All thresholds are denominated in Nigerian Naira (₦). Thresholds apply to the principal licence; subsidiary licences may have additional requirements.
Companies carrying on life assurance business only.
Must maintain an actuarial reserve equal to or greater than 100% of the minimum capital. Solvency margin (assets over liabilities) must meet the RBC ratio prescribed by NAICOM.
Companies carrying on general (non-life) insurance business only.
Must maintain a solvency margin based on the greater of: the prescribed minimum; 20% of net earned premium; or the RBC formula output.
Companies carrying on both life and general insurance under a composite licence. NIIRA 2025 requires composite licensees to maintain clearly ring-fenced life and non-life funds.
Life and non-life funds must be separately maintained and reported. The combined minimum capital reflects the aggregate of life and general thresholds plus a composite premium.
Companies accepting life reinsurance cessions from primary life insurers.
Must comply with the domestic cession framework: capacity must be sufficient to absorb domestic cedants’ retention requirements.
Continental Reinsurance and NRC are the primary domestic reinsurers. Foreign reinsurers are not required to hold capital in Nigeria but must be approved by NAICOM for domestic cessions.
Companies operating a standalone (full) Takaful business (family and/or general Takaful).
Must maintain a Shari’ah-compliant capital structure; Participants’ Risk Account (PRA) and shareholders’ funds must be clearly segregated. SSB required.
Conventional insurers establishing a ring-fenced Takaful window within their existing licence.
The Takaful window must maintain a separate fund structure (PRA) independently of the conventional fund. A Shari’ah Supervisory Board must be appointed.
Technology companies distributing or processing insurance on behalf of a licensed insurer but not assuming insurance risk.
Cannot underwrite risks on own account. Must operate under a formal partnership agreement with a fully licensed insurer. Subject to NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines 2025.
Technology companies holding a full insurance licence and assuming life insurance risk on own account through digital channels.
Subject to all NIIRA 2025 requirements applicable to conventional life insurers, plus additional Insurtech Guidelines requirements (cybersecurity, sandbox pathway, AI/ML governance).
Technology companies holding a full general insurance licence and assuming risk on own account.
Higher capital than life Standalone Insurtech reflects the typically shorter-tail and higher-frequency general insurance risk profile.
Companies specifically licensed to write microinsurance products to low-income policyholders through community, mobile, and cooperative channels.
Restricted to products meeting NAICOM’s microinsurance product parameters (simplified terms, low premium, low sum assured). Cannot write conventional insurance without an additional licence.
₦500,000,000 (Five Hundred Million Naira) plus Professional Indemnity Insurance minimum as prescribed by NAICOM.
Companies acting as brokers placing insurance on behalf of clients.
Must maintain PI insurance coverage as prescribed. Broker capital is in addition to, not in lieu of, the PI insurance requirement.
₦10,000,000 (Ten Million Naira) for corporate agents; individual agents do not have a capital requirement but must hold CIIN Cert. COP.
Corporate entities appointed to distribute insurance products on behalf of licensed insurers.
Corporate agents are not licensed to assume insurance risk. Bancassurance partners are corporate agents of the licenced insurer.
₦20,000,000 (Twenty Million Naira) plus Professional Indemnity Insurance.
Professional firms appointed to assess and report on insurance claims.
PI insurance must be maintained at a minimum indemnity limit prescribed by NAICOM and renewed annually.

blocks.h: Transitional Note: Existing licensed companies that do not meet the NIIRA 2025 minimum capital thresholds at commencement have a phased compliance timeline set out in the NAICOM Recapitalisation Directive. Companies that fail to meet interim milestones are subject to NAICOM enforcement action including restrictions on new business, licence suspension, and ultimately licence revocation.

blocks.text: Table 1D: NAICOM Approved Investment Classes and Portfolio Limits

rows: NIIRA 2025 Part XII; NAICOM Investment Guidelines (subsidiary regulation). Life and general insurance funds are subject to different limit frameworks.

Ensure that insurance funds are invested in assets that are: (1) sufficiently liquid to meet claims obligations; (2) sufficiently diversified to avoid concentration risk; (3) of sufficient credit quality to protect policyholder obligations; and (4) denominated to match policy liabilities.

Limits apply separately to: (a) the Life Fund (all assets backing life policy reserves); (b) the General Fund (assets backing general insurance reserves); and (c) the Shareholders’ Fund (assets held for shareholders’ account above the technical provisions). Takaful window funds are subject to Shari’ah-compliant investment limits.

Only admissible assets count toward the solvency margin calculation. An asset may be held in the portfolio but excluded from the solvency calculation if it fails the admissibility test (e.g., unlisted shares, connected-party loans, impaired assets).
Verify current limits against the most recently published NAICOM Investment Guidelines at naicom.gov.ng. Limits may be updated by NAICOM circular without amendment to NIIRA 2025 itself.
FGN bonds, Treasury bills, FGN Sukuk. Issued by the Debt Management Office (DMO) and traded on FMDQ.
The primary insurance investment asset class in Nigeria. Zero credit risk (sovereign). FGN Sukuk is Shari’ah-compliant for Takaful funds.
Bonds issued by state governments and FCT.
Credit quality varies across states. NAICOM requires investment-grade state bonds only. Limit per issuing state may apply.
Bonds rated investment grade (BBB– or better by an approved rating agency) issued by Nigerian corporates and quoted on NGX or FMDQ.
Rating must be current (within 12 months) from a NAICOM-approved rating agency. Unrated bonds are not admissible.
Ordinary shares of companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange Group.
Must be exchange-listed. Unlisted equity stakes are excluded from admissibility. No single issuer to exceed 5% of the fund. Shariah-screened equities only for Takaful funds.
Direct investment in commercial or residential real estate located in Nigeria.
Yes — admissible within limits (valued by NAICOM-approved valuers)
Independent professional valuation required at least every 2 years. Properties under development limited to 10% of the real estate allocation.
Units in NAICOM-approved Real Estate Investment Trusts listed on NGX.
Provides more liquid real estate exposure than direct investment. Limits are in addition to (not within) the Direct Real Estate limit.
Treasury bills, commercial paper, bankers’ acceptances, certificates of deposit with approved Nigerian banks.
Issuing bank must be a licensed Nigerian bank in good regulatory standing. General funds have higher money market limits reflecting shorter duration liabilities.
Loans to policyholders secured against the surrender value of in-force life policies.
Limited to the lower of: the outstanding surrender value or 90% of the policy reserve. Interest rate governed by the policy conditions.
Bonds and funds financing qualifying infrastructure projects (roads, power, water, telecoms).
Yes — admissible within limits (where listed or NAICOM-approved)
Designed to channel insurance long-term capital into Nigeria’s infrastructure deficit. FGN-backed infrastructure bonds are fully admissible.
First-mortgage loans on residential property in Nigeria.
Loan-to-value (LTV) must not exceed 75%. Mortgage must be first-charge security. Duration mismatch risk must be managed within the overall ALM framework.
Demand deposits and fixed-term deposits with NAICOM-approved Nigerian banks.
Bank must be licensed by the CBN and in good regulatory standing. No single bank concentration to exceed 10% of the fund.
Assets denominated in foreign currencies (USD, GBP, EUR, XOF).
10% of Life Fund (where policy liabilities are denominated in foreign currency)
Foreign currency assets may only be held to match foreign-currency-denominated policy liabilities. Speculative foreign currency positions are not admissible.
Investments in companies owned or controlled by the insurer’s shareholders or directors.
Limited admissibility — requires NAICOM prior approval
NAICOM must approve all connected-party investments above de minimis threshold. Failure to obtain approval results in non-admissibility of the asset.
Equity stakes in companies not listed on a recognised exchange.
May be held in the portfolio but are excluded from the solvency margin calculation. Subject to annual impairment review.
Units in NAICOM-approved mutual funds and collective investment schemes registered with the SEC.
The underlying portfolio of the CIS determines the effective asset class exposure; limits apply on a look-through basis.

blocks.h: ALM Note: Life insurers writing long-duration business (whole life, endowments, annuities) must specifically manage the duration gap between asset and liability cash flows. FGN bonds (the longest-dated admissible fixed-income instrument) are the primary duration-matching tool in the Nigerian market. For annuity writers, the lack of very long-dated (30+ year) FGN bonds creates a residual reinvestment risk that must be managed through the ORSA stress testing framework.
